en: In demonstrating the evils of gambling, it should be said:
"What indeed could a person of sound mind perceive in gambling—that abode of manifold faults, that destroyer of modesty and prosperity—such that his intellect would be drawn to it? (12.1)
In this regard, gambling should be understood as a locus of manifold faults because it gives rise to a multitude of defects. For it is indeed:

a source of joy for enemies, an abode of humiliation, a workshop for the business of enmity, a foundation for deceit and hypocrisy, a procedure for the turbidity of strife, and a receptacle for the refuse of evil.

Gambling is the playground of delusion, the burner of the wealth of virtues, the destroyer of the splendor of humility, the exile of fame, and the seed of calamity through the desire to seize the property of others. 12.2.
Furthermore:
It is the removal of fortitude, the dissolution of tranquility, a thunderbolt to the crop of virtuous conduct, and a wind that sweeps away the dust of the defects of agitation, pride, and greed.
Gambling is the occasion for the staining of virtues, the fuel for the fire of sin, a terrible planet of heedlessness, noisy with the foul chatter of harshness and other evils. (12.3)
Moreover, when indeed could there be well-being for one whose mind is addicted to that? For one devoted to gambling, having won, his mind becomes agitated with pride and does not attain tranquility;
he only increases his craving, which is the nurse of all evils.
Since one who is defeated encounters supreme suffering, for that reason also, a wise man ought not to resort to gambling. || 12.4 ||
Even his own kin reproach him, he incurs the contempt of his friends,
and he is not sought after even in the capacity of a kinsman.
And his wealth goes to utter exhaustion. || 12.5 ||

In this regard, it might be argued as follows: "The loss of wealth for one whose mind is addicted to gambling is indeed not certain. For King Puṣkara won the kingdom by defeating King Nala at dice; Śakuni obtained the wealth of Yudhiṣṭhira as well as his minister Vidura; the Yakṣa Pūrṇaka acquired a wife as a prize; and the Goddess of Victory was won at dice. Therefore, this [consequence]—that there would be a loss of wealth for one whose mind is addicted to gambling—is not certain."
"Therefore, one should indeed pray for the status of a kinsman and should not incur the contempt of friends nor the stigma of being censured by one's own kin.

To this we reply: It is not possible to attain through mere chance an object that results in an abundance of misfortune; for by chance alone, someone might occasionally obtain some small fragment of wealth at gambling.

Generally, however, those whose minds are addicted to gambling are seen wandering the earth like Nala and Yudhiṣṭhira, distressed by imprisonment; having staked their entire fortune there, they possess only tattered, soiled garments insufficient even to cover their loins; their bodies are emaciated by hunger, discolored, and wretched; their hearts are filled with grief and reproach; covered in dust, their appearance is harsh; they are untrustworthy even to their friends, have become objects of the world's contempt, and, intent on various improper acts, they roam about.

Some have even had the joints of their fingers on the hands and feet completely eroded; therefore, this is well known by its prevalence: his enjoyments go to ruin, and from that, the arising of all manner of faults occurs. Furthermore, even one who acquires some measure of wealth through gambling—should he, upon seeing the taste of it, give rise to improper greed and, being deceived by the hope of victory, engage in gambling again, he loses both that initial sum of money and what follows it; thus, this is indeed logically consistent. Even though such a result is established as an absolute certainty...
Wealth may be lost through addiction to gambling;
nevertheless, a wise man should reflect upon this and remain devoted to protecting his virtues. 12.6
When considering whether it would be better for wealth to result from gambling or its loss, and what might be superior between these two,
death would be better for one whose mind remains unimpaired in righteousness.
There is no hoard of wealth that is defiled by the vice of gambling. || 12.7 ||
Moreover:
Having cast aside shame and clearly abandoned reflection on the true Dharma, they have joined with evildoers and opened wide the path to hell.
Having become an object of pity for the wise and having trampled his own reputation underfoot, what would he not do out of a desire for wealth through gambling? (12.8)
In this regard, it might be argued: "The engagement in gambling is for the sake of pleasure, not out of greed for the acquisition of wealth.
To this we reply:
there may indeed be such pleasure through this [gambling].
How could he, who is compassionate toward those possessing a multitude of virtues, even think of them— whose souls are defiled by many kinds of faults— as if they were another's wife? (12.9)
The virtuous desire a delight that is endowed with the qualities of dharma and artha, but not one that is contrary to them;
for having experienced excessive and sinful delight, [one suffers greatly].
He plunges into a delight in the difficult terrains of the lower realms. || 12.10 ||
When death stands ready with old age as his bow and disease as his raised arrows, and when one stands before it bound by the faults of one's own karma, how can there be any delight?
And in rebirth, which is the locus of calamity and toil. || 12.11 ||
Even if there might be some flaw here, what fault could there possibly be for one who engages in this for the sake of fully understanding it?
To this we reply:
"Flaw" (*kalā*) is a collection arising from many faults.
And because he was utterly deluded, there were neither qualities nor actions [in him].
Therefore, one should strive by whatever means possible for the sake of establishing the side of virtue, as well as for the attainment of fame and wealth.
One should not pursue even that which is pleasant if it is characterized by turning away from the path of one's own welfare; however,
one should pursue that in which welfare is deposited, as it were.
Having cast aside one's lack of relish, one should take that medicine accordingly.

Having turned the mind away from sinful acts such as gambling and the like— which yield results that are meaningless, lack happiness, and bring ill repute— because the supreme means of accomplishing one's own welfare is based on the Dharma, which yields the fruits of purpose, happiness, and fame both in this life and after death.
One should be adorned with auspicious giving, self-control, and restraint. || 12.14 ||
Thus it is said.
